newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spot natgas prices soften on NYMEX slump.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spot natgas prices soften on NYMEX slump.

text.p: U.S. spot natural gas prices turned softer Thursday as the expiring July futures faltered and July buyers gradually lowered their bids, sources said.

"The market is watching the screen. People are throwing out low bids to let the producers know they're not interested. It's not really a realistic price," one trader said, noting the anticipated weak demand for the first week in July was giving buyers the advantage.
Louisiana Gulf Coast prices for Friday delivery slipped an average of eight cents to the low-$2.20s per mmBtu, holding a slight premium to July 1 values in the high-teens.
At 1447 EDT, July Henry Hub gas futures stood near the session low at $2.145, down 8.2 cents.
Traders also cited ample storage supplies as another reason for the softening.
American Gas Association reported Wednesday that U.S. gas stocks gained 97 bcf last week, making them about 19 percent over year-ago levels.

In the East, where stocks gained 65 bcf last week, New York city gate prices eased into the $2.50s for Friday. However, temperatures in the region are forecast to remain above normal through at least the weekend.
In the Midwest, next-day prices fell seven cents to $2.04-2.05. The July 1 market was pegged in the low-$2 area, indicating a loss of about 10 cents from June indices.
"People are willing to sell below index," one trader said, adding that producers are most likely expecting an even softer aftermarket.
According to AGA, stocks in the producing region held at 54 percent above a year ago.
In West Texas, Permian prices for Friday dropped eight cents to about $2.00-2.01, while July 1 values were talked just below that at $1.97-2.00.
At the southern California border, next-day prices also carried a two to four cent premium to July 1 around $2.20.
San Juan prices for the most part were in convergence in the low-to-mid $1.90s, traders said.
As storage levels in the West neared year-ago levels, the threat of ample storage supplies dwindled, traders said.
"It's just really not a factor anymore. The driving force will be the heat," one Texas trader said.
Separately, Tropical Storm Carlos, strengthening off Mexico's Pacific Coast, was moving west northwesterly and packing winds of 47 mph and gusts of 60 mph, according to Weather Services Corp.
